title: 132 Arrested in Ludhiana as Punjab Police Dismantles International Cyber Fraud Ring Targeting Americans and Canadians
excerpt: The sprawling tech-support scam ran fake call centres, froze over 300 bank accounts, and funnelled proceeds through a Gujarat-linked hawala network
body:
Punjab Police have arrested 132 individuals in Ludhiana in what officials describe as one of the largest coordinated takedowns of an international cyber fraud network operating from Indian soil. The syndicate, which primarily targeted residents of the United States and Canada, ran fake tech-support call centres that impersonated Microsoft, Amazon, and banking customer service lines to extract money from unsuspecting victims overseas.

The operation followed a well-documented playbook. Callers working from rented offices near Sandhu Tower and Silver Oak in Ludhiana’s commercial district used spoofed US and Canadian phone numbers to contact potential victims, typically elderly residents. They posed as tech-support agents, warning targets that their computers had been compromised by viruses or that their bank accounts had been flagged for suspicious activity. Victims were then guided through remote-access software installations that gave the fraudsters direct control of their machines — and, critically, their online banking credentials.

Once access was secured, money was siphoned through a layered network of mule bank accounts. Investigators found that the proceeds were routed through shell companies before being converted to cash via a hawala network with links to Gujarat. Police recovered Rs 1.07 crore in cash from the Ludhiana sites alone, along with laptops, multiple SIM cards, and call-scripting documents that detailed exactly how operatives should respond to common victim objections.

Authorities froze over 300 bank accounts connected to the fraud ring and said the total amount defrauded from overseas victims is still being calculated but is expected to run into several crore. The 132 arrests on May 15 followed weeks of surveillance, with separate raids also yielding Rs 2.05 crore in hawala money from linked operations in Phagwara.

This bust is the latest in a string of large-scale cyber fraud crackdowns across Punjab. Earlier this year, Mohali police arrested 155 suspects across two separate fake call centres in the city’s Industrial Area, while Chandigarh Cyber Police dismantled a network that had duped a senior citizen of Rs 52 lakh through fake TRAI and Enforcement Directorate impersonation.

For Non-Resident Indians in North America, these busts hit uncomfortably close to home — in both directions. Many of the victims are elderly Americans and Canadians who may live in the same neighbourhoods, attend the same community centres, and shop at the same grocery stores as members of the Indian diaspora. When headlines link “India” and “scam call centres,” the reputational spillover affects the broader community, feeding stereotypes that Indian-American advocacy groups have spent years pushing back against.

At the same time, the fraud operations themselves are built on the same English-language fluency and technical literacy that the Indian diaspora is celebrated for. The irony is not lost on community leaders: the same talent pipeline that produces Silicon Valley engineers also produces, at its margins, globally competitive scam operations.

Punjab’s Director General of Police has signalled that the Ludhiana bust is part of a broader, state-wide campaign against cyber fraud networks, with cooperation from the FBI and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police on victim identification and evidence sharing. India’s Enforcement Directorate is separately investigating the hawala channels for money-laundering violations.

For NRIs, the practical takeaway is familiar but worth repeating: never grant remote access to anyone who calls unsolicited claiming to be from a tech company or bank. US and Canadian authorities, along with Microsoft and Amazon themselves, have repeatedly stated that they will never cold-call users to report security issues. The best defence against these operations — which are growing more sophisticated by the month — remains a healthy scepticism of any unexpected phone call that creates a sense of urgency.
